thread:
jess: Heads up — customer TYCO (eu-west) is reporting intermittent failures to our edge. Their firewall logs show dropped TCP because the source port keeps changing during our healthchecks and LB probes. They asked for a "short, stable allowlist". :wave:
omar: Can you paste what IPs we see as source when their requests hit our edges? I pulled logs but want to confirm region mapping.
jess: From our edge logs the egress IPs for eu-west on the public side (healthcheck / probe traffic) are currently: 203.0.113.96/28 and 198.51.100.32/29 — that's the set the load balancers and health agents use. Note: these are NAT source IPs from our outbound pool, not per-instance.
maria: Important detail: the customer's firewall is only allowing a narrow ephemeral port range (1024-5000) and then doing stateful inspection. Our SNAT changed source ports outside that range and the firewall closed the flows midhandshake.
kai: Two quick options: allow the entire cidr blocks (recommended) OR if they can't, ask them to broaden allowed ephemeral port range to 1024-65535 for outgoing connections to our IPs. Also avoid strict TCP sequence validation in middleboxes for health probes.
jess: Sent customer a minimal snippet they can drop into their ACLs. Also flagged that if their proxy performs TLS MITM, the SNI might be rewritten and cause x509 failures.
omar: Adding the note we should provide a downloadable, signed JSON for these IP blocks that they can programmatically consume (and clear cache headers). Ops-bot, do we have a published egress manifest URL?
ops-bot: We publish region egress manifests at https://status.redwood.example/egress-manifests.json (v1). Current eu-west blocklist: ["203.0.113.96/28","198.51.100.32/29"]. Manifest supports `expires_at` and `signed_by`.
maria: Also callout: if they run outbound proxy chaining (customer-proxy -> outbound fw), ensure the proxy preserves destination IP in ACL logs; some proxies rewrite to internal IP and the firewall sees only proxy IP.
kai: For customers that must restrict by FQDN instead of IPs, recommend validating that their firewall supports TLS SNI allowlists (and not interception). If they use DNS-based allowlisting, note our edge IPs can rotate during scale events — recommend using the manifest with automated updates.
jess: I told the customer: 1) allow those two CIDRs in their egress allowlist for destination port 80/443 and for healthcheck ports 10256 (k8s-style probes) if they inspect them, 2) expand ephemeral port range on their firewall to 1024-65535 when talking to our edges, 3) if using a proxy, add our manifest URL as a trusted-source and whitelist the proxy's CONNECT semantics.
omar: One more gotcha — some enterprise firewalls do port-preserving SNAT under high-concurrency which can lead to port exhaustion. If they see source port collision, recommend enabling SNAT port pooling or assign a dedicated NAT pool for our egress.
maria: Customer asked about TLS active inspection. Short answer: if they intercept TLS, they must allowlist the hostname (or bypass) for our health endpoints, because cert validation will fail otherwise.
kai: I'm adding a small curl test they can run from their proxy box to validate connectivity:
```
curl -v --resolve edge.redwood.example:443:203.0.113.97 https://edge.redwood.example/healthz
```
If that works, they can programmatically verify routing + TLS.
jess: OK I'm going to send the manifest URL plus a one-line RFC-style blurb for the firewall team. Will include both CIDRs and the recommended ephemeral port expansion. :thumbsup:
ops-bot: Created ticket INF-5923 (egress-manifest:eu-west) and scheduled a weekly rotation check.
maria: Thanks — please tell them to ping here if they need an allowlist signed JWK for automation.
omar: Nice. If this pattern repeats we'll include an email template in the customer onboarding docs.
jess: Closing loop: customer confirmed after widening ephemeral ports the failures stopped. Leaving this thread for the KB write-up.
